title: Salomon vs Merrell Hiking Shoes: Why Your Foot Shape Decides It
meta_title: Salomon vs Merrell: Which Is Better on 5 Kenyan Trails?
meta_description: Salomon vs Merrell hiking shoes compared: fit, weight, grip and waterproofing, matched to five trails near Nairobi, plus what to check on a thrifted pair.
excerpt: Salomon vs Merrell comes down to foot shape: Salomon for slim feet and fast, rocky hikes, Merrell for wide feet and long, comfortable days on Kenyan trails.
content:
Foot shape settles most Salomon vs Merrell decisions long before price or brand loyalty does. Salomon builds close-fitting, lighter shoes with a locked-in heel that suit narrow feet and quick walking on rocky ground. Merrell builds roomier, softer shoes that feel comfortable from the first step and suit wider feet on steady day hikes.

Both brands turn up constantly on Kenyan trails and on thrifted shoe racks in Nairobi, often side by side, which makes the choice harder rather than easier. Below we compare the flagship models using the brands' own specs, explain how each fits, and match them to five trails within reach of the city.

Quick Facts

  • Origins: Salomon began in 1947 in Annecy, France; Merrell made its first boot in 1981 and has belonged to Wolverine World Wide since 1997.
  • Flagships: most Salomon vs Merrell comparisons pit the X Ultra 5 GORE-TEX against the Moab 3 GORE-TEX.
  • Weight: about 380 g per shoe for the X Ultra 5 GORE-TEX; about 460 g per shoe for the wide-fit Moab 3 GORE-TEX.
  • Drop: 11.5 mm on the Moab 3; reviewers measure about 11 mm on the X Ultra 5.
  • Fit: Salomon runs snug and narrow in the forefoot; Merrell runs roomy. Both sell wide versions.
  • Kenyan sweet spot: day hikes near Nairobi; for loaded treks on Mt Kenya, step up to a stiffer boot.

Is Salomon or Merrell Better for Kenyan Trails?

Neither side of the Salomon vs Merrell question wins outright. Salomon is better for fast hiking on rocky, technical ground and for slim feet. Merrell is better for comfort on long, steady days, for beginners and for wider feet. Your foot and your trail decide it.

Salomon grew out of Alpine skiing and trail running, so its hiking shoes feel low, precise and quick. Merrell began with hand-built boots and kept a comfort-first character in the Moab, which Merrell's own brand history calls the world's number one hiking boot.

On Longonot's ash-covered climb, a light shoe that grips your heel saves effort, which favours Salomon. On a six-hour Ngong Hills ridge walk, a shoe that never pinches matters more.

X Ultra 5 vs Moab 3: the everyday hiking shoes

These two low-cut shoes sit at the heart of the Salomon vs Merrell debate. The X Ultra 5 is lighter and steadier from side to side, so it feels secure on tilted rock; Salomon's X Ultra 5 GORE-TEX page lists it for rocky, technical terrain on full-day hikes. The Moab 3 is heavier but softer, with a bellows tongue against grit and a cushioned heel for hard murram roads.

Quest 4 vs Moab 3 Mid: when you need a boot

For Mt Kenya, the Salomon vs Merrell comparison moves up to boots: the Quest 4 GORE-TEX against the Moab 3 Mid. The Quest is a proper trekking boot of about 650 g, with a nubuck and textile upper, a toe cap and a firm chassis. Under a 10-12 kg pack on the scree below Point Lenana (4,985 m), it gives far more support. The Moab 3 Mid stays a soft boot, better for wet-season day hikes with a light load.

How Do Salomon and Merrell Fit Differently?

Salomon fits close, with a locked heel and a fairly narrow forefoot. Merrell fits generously, with more room around the toes. If one brand has ever pinched your little toe, start the Salomon vs Merrell search with the other.

Salomon's SensiFit upper wraps the foot from midsole to laces, which slim feet love and broad feet often find tight. Merrell's Moab fits most feet out of the box and comes in medium and wide widths. In any Salomon vs Merrell fitting, walk down a slope or some stairs before you decide.

Which brand suits wide feet?

Merrell usually suits wide feet better, especially a Moab 3 wide-width model. If you prefer Salomon, try the X Ultra 5 Wide, because the standard version is noticeably narrower across the forefoot.

Long descents such as Longonot's crater wall push your foot forward, so leave a thumb's width in front of your longest toe. Our guide to hiking boot sizes in Kenya explains how UK, EU and US labels line up.

Quicklace or traditional laces?

Salomon's quickLACE tightens in one pull and never comes undone, but it pulls evenly along the whole foot, which can bother a high instep. Merrell's ordinary laces let you loosen the forefoot and lock the ankle separately, a small point that often settles the choice for hikers with fussy feet.

Salomon vs Merrell Grip: Which Is Better in Mud, Dust and Rock?

Merrell's Vibram TC5+ sole grips dry murram, grass and rock dependably. Salomon's Contagrip performs well on loose dirt and steep descents, though some reviewers find it less sure on smooth, wet rock. Neither flagship is a mud specialist.

The long rains (roughly March to May) and short rains (roughly October to December) turn red soil and black cotton soil around Nairobi into grease, and both flagships clog in deep clay. For muddy months, Salomon's Speedcross trail runner, with 5 mm Mud Contagrip lugs, bites harder than either. In the dusty dry months, the Salomon vs Merrell grip gap almost disappears and fit decides again.

Which brand is more waterproof in the short rains?

On waterproofing, Salomon vs Merrell is a draw for GORE-TEX models, because both use the same membrane. Merrell's "Waterproof" models use the brand's own membrane, and "Vented" Moabs are not waterproof at all, so read the tongue label.

No low shoe stops water pouring in over the collar. For the Aberdares or a muddy Ngong ridge in November, add waterproof leg gaiters to whichever shoe you choose.

Salomon vs Merrell by Trail: Five Hikes Near Nairobi

Match the shoe to the ground you will walk on most.

  1. Karura Forest, Nairobi: about 5 km of firm paths on the yellow loop. Either brand works.
  2. Ngong Hills ridge, about 11 km: grassy, rolling walking where Merrell's cushioning shines, unless rain has made the grass greasy.
  3. Mt Longonot crater rim, about 13.5 km: loose ash and two steep climbs. Salomon's lighter weight and heel hold give it the edge.
  4. Hell's Gate, Elsa Gate to the gorge: about 8 km of gravel, then rock steps in the gorge, where Salomon's chassis feels steadier.
  5. Elephant Hill, Aberdares: deep mud and bamboo. Choose a mid-cut boot from either brand, plus gaiters.

What Should You Check on a Second-Hand Pair in Nairobi?

Check the midsole, the lugs, the lining and the fastening. On Salomon, look at the quickLACE cord and toggle; on Merrell, look at the suede where the toe flexes. A sound midsole matters more than a clean upper.

For most Nairobi hikers, the Salomon vs Merrell choice happens at a thrifted rail, not a shop window. Quality pre-owned pairs often have plenty of trail life left and make GORE-TEX far more affordable. Before you pay:

  • Midsole: deep creases or foam that feels hard and brittle point to an old pair.
  • Lugs: the forefoot lugs should still have sharp edges.
  • Lining: holes inside the heel mean the waterproofing is gone.
  • Label: the tongue label shows the model, size and GORE-TEX, Waterproof or Vented.

Pro Tips for the Salomon vs Merrell Choice

  • If your toes touch the front on a downhill step, go up half a size.
  • Choose GORE-TEX for the rainy months and a vented Moab for January-February.
  • Break any pair in on a Karura loop before Longonot or the Aberdares.
  • Wear merino wool hiking socks to cut blisters on long descents.
  • Dry muddy shoes slowly, away from direct heat; our boot care tips explain why.

Frequently Asked Questions

Salomon vs Merrell: which is better for beginners?

Merrell is usually the easier brand for beginners. A Moab 3 needs almost no breaking in, fits a wide range of feet and is forgiving on steady day hikes such as Karura or the Ngong Hills. Salomon suits beginners with slim feet who want a lighter, more precise shoe, but try it on first.

Do Salomon shoes run smaller than Merrell?

Salomon shoes often feel smaller than Merrell in the same size because the forefoot is narrower and the fit snugger, not because the length differs much. Many hikers go half a size up in Salomon for thick socks and long descents. Merrell usually fits true to size or slightly roomy.

Salomon vs Merrell: which one lasts longer?

Both brands last a similar time on similar trails, and the outsole and midsole usually wear out before the upper. Merrell's suede ages gracefully, while Salomon's synthetic Matryx upper resists abrasion well. How often you hike, the rock you walk on and how you dry your shoes matter more than which side of Salomon vs Merrell you pick.

Can I climb Mt Kenya in Salomon or Merrell hiking shoes?

Low Salomon or Merrell hiking shoes are not ideal for a Mt Kenya summit climb with a loaded pack. They lack the ankle support and warmth for frozen scree near Point Lenana at 4,985 m. A trekking boot such as the Salomon Quest 4 GORE-TEX is the better choice, while a Moab 3 Mid can work for light day hikes lower down.

Does the Salomon vs Merrell choice change for wide feet?

Yes. For wide feet, the Salomon vs Merrell choice usually tips towards Merrell, whose Moab 3 comes in medium and wide widths with a roomy toe box. Salomon also makes Wide versions of the X Ultra 5, which suit some broader feet. Try both on with hiking socks, ideally late in the day.

Final Thoughts

Slim feet and fast, rocky hikes point to Salomon; broad feet and long, comfortable days point to Merrell. Both make dependable GORE-TEX shoes for the trails around Nairobi, and both need a proper boot for Mt Kenya. Settle Salomon vs Merrell by trying the two shapes back to back, then take the winner round a Karura loop before your next big hike.
